Transforms move mass, not points A transform of a random variable moves probability mass, and the only honest way to follow it is to track a small segment, never a point. This is the dx view from pdf-and-cdf-basics doing real work. The warm-up was W = -Z. My flipping argument: negation literally maps z = -k to +k, so the PDF flips over 0, and \varphi is even, so W \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) too. The argument is valid, but it rests on a hidden lemma worth saying out loud: negation carries the mass \varphi(z)\,dz sitting on [-k-dk, -k] onto [k, k+dk], an interval of the same width. Rigid transport, no stretching, so heights carry over unchanged. (The CDF route needs no picture at all: P(-Z \le w) = P(Z \ge -w) = 1 - \Phi(-w) = \Phi(w). Two moves.) The width caveat is the whole story. Run the same flip on W = Z^3 and it breaks: the segment [k, k+dk] lands on [k^3, (k+dk)^3], whose width is 3k^2\,dk to first order. The width multiplier is the derivative of the map. To keep the mass block's area fixed, the height divides by that same factor: f_W(k^3) = \varphi(k)/3k^2. Near 0, where 3k^2 < 1, widths compress and the density piles up instead. That is the U^2 pile-up from sitting 1, now with a formula behind it. The general Normal is defined by this transport. Take X = \mu + \sigma Z in two stages. Stretch: w = \sigma z scales every width dz by \sigma, so heights divide by \sigma, giving f_W(w) = \varphi(w/\sigma)/\sigma. Shift: sliding by \mu moves the curve without touching widths, giving f_X(x) = \varphi\!\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\frac{1}{\sigma}. Why \varphi(w/\sigma) and not \varphi(w)? Read it from the new variable's side. The height that lived at z now lives at w = \sigma z, so the density at w is the original looked up at its preimage w/\sigma: from w's perspective, w = 1 holds whatever lived at z = 1/\sigma. The shift is the same logic, the mass at x came from w = x - \mu. The recipe for any one-to-one Y = g(X): evaluate the old density at the preimage, then divide by the stretch factor |g'|. Standardization and the 68-95-99.7 rule The transport also runs backwards: if X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) then (X-\mu)/\sigma \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1), and consequently F(x) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right). There is only one Normal, and every Normal question becomes a \Phi question. For quick mental math: P(|Z| < 1) \approx 0.68, P(|Z| < 2) \approx 0.95, P(|Z| < 3) \approx 0.997. The worked pipeline: X \sim \mathcal{N}(-1, 4), find P(|X| < 3). First trap dodged: the second parameter is the variance, so \sigma = 2, not 4. Standardizing turns -3 < X < 3 into -1 < Z < 2, so the exact answer is \Phi(2) - \Phi(-1) = \Phi(2) + \Phi(1) - 1 by the tail identity. For the approximation, my decomposition: [-3, -1] is the left half of the 1SD band (0.34) and [-1, 3] is the right half of the 2SD band (0.475), total 0.815 against a true 0.8186. The bands measure from \mu = -1, not from 0. That is exactly what standardizing guards against. The crypto anchor: Gaussians carry lattice crypto. Falcon samples discrete Gaussians, LWE hides secrets under Gaussian noise, and the security arguments are tail bounds, the 68-95-99.7 rule taken to cryptographic extremes. The Exponential from its survival function The Exponential \text{Expo}(\lambda) models the waiting time until the first arrival when arrivals hit at rate \lambda. My recall worry ("doesn't e^{-\lambda x} blow up on the left?") is answered by the story: waits are never negative, the support is (0, \infty), and the blow-up region is simply not in it. The kernel e^{-\lambda x} needs a constant, and unlike the Normal's \sqrt{2\pi} this one is a freshman integral: c = \lambda, so f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \quad x > 0. Units sanity check: \lambda carries per-time units, exactly the density units a PDF over time must have, and \lambda x in the exponent is dimensionless. The CDF is F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}, so the survival function is P(X > x) = e^{-\lambda x}. That survival function is the real primitive: exponential-survival-first rebuilds it from nothing but a constant rate, and everything below runs through it. The mean and variance come from the chapter's signature move, compute for the simplest family member and transform out. One integration by parts gives E(X) = 1 for \text{Expo}(1), and taking E(X^2) = 2 on faith gives \text{Var}(X) = 1. Scaling is the family's only knob (a shift would drag the support off (0,\infty), so unlike the Normal there is no location part): X/\lambda \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda), with mean 1/\lambda and variance 1/\lambda^2. Faster arrivals, shorter waits. One flag from my own work: I wrote \text{Var} = E(X^2) - E(X) and got the right number only because E(X) = 1 is its own square. The formula is E(X^2) - (E(X))^2. Cheap luck, flagged. Memorylessness Memoryless property A continuous distribution on (0,\infty) is memoryless if for all s, t \ge 0: P(X \ge s + t \mid X \ge s) = P(X \ge t) Given you have already waited s without success, the chance of surviving another t is a fresh start. The past s is erased. The proof is two lines once you see the collapse: the event X > s+t implies X > s, so their intersection is just the smaller event, and the conditional becomes a ratio of survivals: P(X > s+t \mid X > s) = \frac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}} = e^{-\lambda t}. What the whole proof rests on, in one sentence: exponential functions have the property f(x+y) = f(x) \cdot f(y). The survival function factorizes, so conditioning divides the past out exactly. No polynomial or Gaussian tail survives that ratio unchanged. And the converse holds: any continuous distribution on (0,\infty) whose survival function satisfies G(s+t) = G(s)G(t) is forced to be e^{-\lambda x} for some \lambda. So the Exponential is the only memoryless continuous distribution. Memorylessness characterizes it. The Poisson bridge Poisson process with rate λ Arrivals land on a timeline such that the number of arrivals in any interval of length t is \text{Pois}(\lambda t), and counts in disjoint intervals are independent. The definition speaks only the counting language (how many arrivals, a discrete number). The waiting language is one sentence away: "the first arrival has not happened by time t" is the same event as "zero arrivals landed in (0, t]". Identical events have identical probabilities, so P(T_1 > t) = P(N_t = 0) = e^{-\lambda t}\frac{(\lambda t)^0}{0!} = e^{-\lambda t}. The Exponential survival function falls out of a definition that never mentioned waiting: T_1 \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda). After the first arrival, independence of disjoint intervals restarts the process fresh, so the gaps between arrivals are i.i.d. \text{Expo}(\lambda). (Disjoint is doing the work there: overlapping intervals share arrivals, so their counts are obviously dependent.) One process, two views: count the arrivals and you get Poisson, time them and you get Exponential. That is why they share the letter \lambda. The units wire I crossed twice before it settled: \lambda is a rate (arrivals per unit time), E(T_1) = 1/\lambda is a time. Reciprocals, not equals. Buses at rate 6 per hour have mean gap 1/6 hour, and 6 \ne 1/6. They coincide only at \lambda = 1, the deceptive special case. The other \lambda, the prefactor in \lambda e^{-\lambda t}, is the same letter doing a second consistent job: the density's per-time units showing up for work. Bitcoin runs on this bridge. Block arrivals are engineered into a Poisson process (difficulty retargets to hold \lambda = 1/10 per minute), inter-block gaps are \text{Expo}(1/10), and memorylessness is what "progress-free mining" means. After 25 minutes without a block, the expected wait is still 10 minutes from now. A block is never "due". What stayed shaky: Fred's bus paradox Buses in Blotchville have Expo gaps with mean 10 minutes, Fred arrives at a random moment, and memorylessness resets the clock: his expected wait is a fresh 10 minutes. His friend argues 5, and each premise sounds fine (you land uniformly inside a gap, the average gap is 10, so you wait half of it). The part I did get: with alternating 50/5 gaps, the dart lands in a 50-minute gap ten times more often, so the gap containing Fred is systematically longer than a typical gap. Length-biased sampling. Which sentence of the friend's argument actually dies, and how the two answers reconcile, is parked as fred-bus-waiting-paradox and opens sitting 3.

Two statements look almost identical, yet only one proves a function is one-to-one. The definition is f(x_1) = f(x_2) \implies x_1 = x_2: assume the outputs are equal, deduce the inputs were equal. The tempting lookalike just flips it to f(x_1) 
eq f(x_2) \implies x_1 
eq x_2: different outputs came from different inputs. Both seem to say distinct things stay distinct, so why does the first prove one-to-one and the second prove nothing about it? Where I got stuck I read the first statement as the definition and the second as an obvious twin of it. Both talk about two inputs and two outputs staying apart. I could not see why the direction of the implication, which side you assume and which side you conclude, decides whether you have proved one-to-one at all. They felt like the same claim written two ways. Statement 2 never tests a collision Statement 2 fails because it only ever looks at outputs that are already different, and a one-to-one function breaks at the outputs that are the same. Picture statement 2 in action. It pairs one input to an output, and a second input to a different output. Both inputs are distinct, both outputs are distinct, the statement is satisfied. But nothing stops a third input from landing on one of those two outputs. That third arrow is a collision, two inputs sharing one output, which is exactly a many-to-one function. Statement 2 never looks there, so a many-to-one function sails right through it. The definition does the opposite. It starts at a shared output and forces the two inputs to be equal. It walks straight up to the collision and rules it out. That is why it eliminates the whole many-to-one subset and leaves only one-to-one behind. Take f(x) = x^2 on the reals, which is not one-to-one since f(3) = f(-3) = 9. Feed it to statement 2 and pick two different outputs, say 16 and 25. Their inputs 4 and 5 are different, so the statement holds. It held, and the function is still many-to-one. The collision at 9, where 3 and -3 meet, sits in a blind spot statement 2 never visits. Statement 2 is the converse in disguise Statement 2 is not the contrapositive of the definition. It is the inverse, and the inverse is logically equivalent to the converse, not the original. One implication between input-equality and output-equality has four forms. Write the definition as the original, and the rest fall out: StatementLogical roleWhat it provesf(x_1)=f(x_2) \implies x_1=x_2original (statement 1)one-to-onex_1 
eq x_2 \implies f(x_1) 
eq f(x_2)contrapositive (statement 3)one-to-onex_1 = x_2 \implies f(x_1)=f(x_2)conversejust being a functionf(x_1) 
eq f(x_2) \implies x_1 
eq x_2inverse (statement 2)just being a function The original and its contrapositive are equivalent, so statement 1 and statement 3 both prove one-to-one. The converse and the inverse are equivalent too, and statement 2 is the inverse. So statement 2 says exactly what its converse twin says: x_1 = x_2 \implies f(x_1) = f(x_2), same input gives the same output. That is not one-to-one. It is just well-definedness, the rule that one input maps to exactly one output, which is what makes f a function in the first place. It is the deterministic-output property, and every function obeys it, many-to-one ones included. So it cannot tell one-to-one functions apart from the rest. The handle Of the four implications, the original and its contrapositive prove one-to-one. The converse and the inverse only prove you have a function at all. Statement 2 is the inverse, so it lives in the wrong half. To actually prove one-to-one, assume the outputs are equal (statement 1) or assume the inputs differ (statement 3). This is the same deterministic-output rule that blocks an inverse when a function is not one-to-one, the other half of what makes a function bijective. See onto-functions for the onto side of that story.

Onto (surjective) A function f: A \to B is onto if for every y \in B there exists at least one x \in A with f(x) = y. Every target in the codomain gets hit, so the range fills B completely with no unreachable outputs. The whole question onto answers is simple: can every output be produced? Pick any y you like in the codomain, and onto promises some input maps to it. Geometrically, for f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, the graph has to touch every height on the y-axis. No gaps, no unreachable y. Proving onto: run the definition backwards The definition reads "for every y, there exists an x", so the proof always has the same four moves. Start with an arbitrary y \in B. Solve f(x) = y for x in terms of y. Check that this x actually lands in the domain A. Then plug it back and confirm f(x) really simplifies to y. For f(x) = 2x - 3 on \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, the candidate input is x = (y+3)/2, which is real for any real y, and substituting it back gives y. That is the recipe in full: find the preimage, check it lives in the domain, verify it maps where you want. Not-onto, and what it does not mean The cheapest not-onto function is f(x) = 1 on \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}. Every input is used, but the output is just \{1\}, so the rest of \mathbb{R} is never reached. The function f(x) = x^2 misses every negative number the same way. Both are perfectly valid functions, they just fail to cover their codomain. Outputs may have gaps, inputs never can I first read "not onto" as the function being allowed to skip some inputs, leaving part of the domain unused. That mixes up the two sides. A function is total by definition: every element of its stated domain must map somewhere. If a rule is undefined at a point, that point is not in the domain (1/x has domain \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}, not \mathbb{R}). Onto is about the other side, whether the outputs cover B. Outputs are free to leave gaps, which is exactly what not-onto means. Inputs are not. Why onto is worth proving Two reasons. First, guaranteed solvability. Onto is an existence theorem in disguise: if f is onto, the equation f(x) = y has a solution for every y. In linear algebra, a transformation T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m being onto is exactly the statement that Ax = b is solvable for every b. Second, onto is half of what you need for an inverse. To build f^{-1}: B \to A, the inverse has to be defined on all of B, because a function is total on its domain. If f is not onto, some y \in B has no preimage, so f^{-1} has nothing to send it to and fails to be a function. Onto is only half of an inverse Onto gives every y at least one preimage. For an inverse you also need at most one, which is the one-to-one (injective) condition: no output is shared by two inputs, or f^{-1} would have to send one y to two places and stop being deterministic. Onto plus one-to-one is bijective, exactly one preimage per y, and that is when f^{-1} exists. The one-to-one side, and the trap that catches most people proving it, is its own story in one-to-one-proof-converse-trap. Equal sizes collapse onto and one-to-one When the domain and codomain are finite and the same size, |A| = |B| = n, onto and one-to-one stop being separate properties. Prove one and the other comes free. The reason is the Pigeonhole Principle: if f is not one-to-one, two inputs collide on one output, so the n inputs cover at most n-1 outputs, leaving some element of B unreached, which is not onto. Run it the other way and not-onto forces not one-to-one. Infinite sets break this. Take f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} with f(1) = 1 and f(n) = n - 1 for n > 1. It is not one-to-one, since 1 and 2 both map to 1, yet it is onto, since every y has preimage y + 1. The bound that locked the two properties together is gone. This asymmetry is the very definition of an infinite set: a set is infinite exactly when it has a map to itself that is onto but not one-to-one (a Dedekind-infinite set). The handle Onto is a claim about the output side: every target in B gets hit. Inputs are never allowed gaps, that is what makes f a function. Outputs are allowed gaps, that is what makes a function not-onto, and onto closes that gap. Add one-to-one and the inverse appears. For equal finite sizes the two properties come as a pair, for infinite sets they part ways.

The sitting in one line For a continuous random variable, probability lives on small segments, never on points. The density is the CDF's slope, f = F', every probability is an area under f, and any single point carries exactly zero. From staircase to ramp In the discrete world (probability-distributions-and-random-variables) the CDF is a staircase and the PMF lives in the jumps: P(X = x) = F(x) - F(x^-), the jump height at x. A continuous CDF is a smooth ramp with no jumps at all. Apply the same jump formula and it forces P(X = x) = 0 for every single x. Nothing is left over for any individual point. The interesting part is what falls out on the way. Writing the small difference at x gives F'(x)\,dx, and as dx \rightarrow 0 \implies P(X = x) = F'(x).dx \rightarrow 0. It is the chapter's central object: f(x) = F'(x), the probability density function. One cheap consequence worth pocketing: since endpoints carry zero, P(a < X < b) = P(a \le X \le b), and every half-open version in between. No more < vs \le anxiety. Probability lives on segments (the dx view) f(x) is not a probability. f(x)\,dx is: the probability that X lands in a tiny window of width dx around x. Density is probability per unit length, which means it carries units. My waiting-time example: X uniform on half an hour has density height 2 measured in hours and height 1/30 measured in minutes. Same random variable, same probabilities, different heights. Only height times width is real. That also settles why a density can exceed 1. The only validity conditions are f \ge 0 everywhere and total area 1. Height 2 (or 3, or 100) is fine as long as the support is narrow enough. \text{Unif}(0, 1/3) sits at height 3 everywhere and is a perfectly legal distribution. The mantra: height is probability per unit length, only area is probability. The same view is the right way to think about transformations. To understand Y = g(X), don't ask where a point goes, ask what happens to a small segment. The map g sends [x, x + dx] to a segment around g(x), and the probability mass f(x)\,dx riding on it is conserved. If the segment gets stretched, that mass spreads over more length, so the density drops. Compressed, the density rises. 3blue1brown has a video on exactly this segment intuition, from his probability playlist. Working with densities The practical workflow: differentiate the CDF when you want the shape, use the CDF directly when you want a probability. The Rayleigh warm-up shows both. Its CDF is F(x) = 1 - e^{-x^2/2} for x > 0, so the density is f(x) = x\,e^{-x^2/2} by the chain rule, and the tail needs no integral at all: P(X > 2) = 1 - F(2) = e^{-2}. The CDF already did the integrating. Everything from the discrete world translates with one mechanical dictionary: sums become integrals, P(X = x) becomes f(x)\,dx. So E(X) = \int x\,f(x)\,dx and LOTUS reads E(g(X)) = \int g(x)\,f(x)\,dx. Linearity, LOTUS, and the variance identity from lotus-and-variance all carry over unchanged. The Uniform \text{Unif}(a, b) formalizes "a completely random number between a and b": a flat density f(x) = 1/(b-a) on the support, forced by area 1, and a ramp CDF F(x) = (x-a)/(b-a) there. My first CDF attempt failed the standard sanity checks, so they are worth naming: F must be 0 at the left edge, 1 at the right edge, and it must stay at those values outside the support. Writing "0 otherwise" claims P(U \le 5) = 0 for \text{Unif}(0,1), which no CDF can do. For U \sim \text{Unif}(0,1), probability literally is length: P(U \in (0.2, 0.5)) = 0.3. Its moments are E(U) = 1/2 and \text{Var}(U) = 1/12. The general case needs zero new integrals: a + (b-a)U \sim \text{Unif}(a,b) (stretch, then shift), so E = (a+b)/2 and \text{Var} = (b-a)^2/12. The variance contains only the width b - a. Where the interval sits doesn't matter, only how wide the room is. Same support is not same distribution: the U² trap A friend argues: U^2 still lands in (0,1), so it is still completely random there. The test comes from the Uniform section: completely random means flat PDF, which means linear CDF. Compute it: P(U^2 \le x) = P(U \le \sqrt{x}) = \sqrt{x}. Not linear. Same support, different distribution. The segment view says where the mass went. Squaring pulls every value in (0,1) downward, compressing segments near 0, so the density piles up there. About 70% of draws land below 1/2, since \sqrt{1/2} \approx 0.707. This is exactly the classic nonce-bias bug in ECDSA and Schnorr. Reduce a uniform 256-bit number mod the group order n and every residue is still possible, but residues below 2^{256} \bmod n get hit slightly more often. The support looks fine, the distribution is not uniform, and with enough signatures lattice attacks turn that tiny skew into the secret key. The flat-PDF test is the formal version of the check that catches it. Universality of the Uniform One theorem, two directions, both riding on the Uniform's special property: its CDF is the identity, P(U \le p) = p, so U can hand you an event of any probability you name. Universality of the Uniform Let F be a continuous, strictly increasing CDF and let U \sim \text{Unif}(0,1). Then: Manufacture. X = F^{-1}(U) is a random variable whose CDF is exactly F. Flatten. If X is a random variable with CDF F, then F(X) \sim \text{Unif}(0,1). Direction 1: F^{-1}(U) has CDF F. I want X = g(U) with P(X \le x) = F(x). Solve for g instead of verifying a given answer: P(g(U) \le x) = P(U \le g^{-1}(x)) = g^{-1}(x), so matching against F(x) forces g^{-1} = F, that is X = F^{-1}(U). The first step silently used that g is increasing, which is why the theorem assumes F strictly increasing. My own reading of what the proof does: we have a family of events \{X \le x\} whose probabilities we want to be F(x). The Uniform has the special property P(U \le u) = u, so in particular P(U \le F(x)) = F(x), an event with exactly the right probability, sitting there pre-made. Setting X = F^{-1}(U) just lines \{X \le x\} up with \{U \le F(x)\}. The important property is realizing P(U \le F(x)) = F(x). That is the core of the proof. The percentile reading makes the result feel obvious: a CDF converts values to percentiles, F^{-1} is the percentile-to-value lookup, and to draw from any distribution you draw a percentile uniformly and look up which value owns it. The picture is uniform rain on the percentile axis: Where F is steep, a wide band of percentiles gets squeezed into a narrow window of values, so landings pile up exactly where the density is tall. The slope F' = f is the local compression ratio of this transport, the segment view from above, one more time. And U^2 was already this machine running: target F(x) = \sqrt{x} gives F^{-1}(u) = u^2. Direction 2: F(X) \sim \text{Unif}(0,1). Feed X into its own CDF and it flattens, whatever distribution X had. One line, using that a strictly increasing F makes \{F(X) \le u\} and \{X \le F^{-1}(u)\} the same event: P(F(X) \le u) = P(X \le F^{-1}(u)) = F(F^{-1}(u)) = u. You never invert F inside a probability, you just rename the event: both descriptions represent the same values underneath, because F is a simple one-one mapping x \to F(x). Strict monotonicity is what makes the renaming valid in both directions. Why (0,1) and not some \text{Unif}(a,b)? In direction 2 it is forced: F outputs probabilities, so F(X) physically lives in [0,1]. In direction 1 it is just the canonical choice. From a V \sim \text{Unif}(a,b) source, standardize first and use X = F^{-1}\big((V-a)/(b-a)\big). Direction 1 is what simulation libraries call inverse transform sampling: computers only generate uniform bits, and this is how uniform bits become samples from anything with a tractable F^{-1}. What stayed shaky The sitting's one real miss: I claimed neither probability nor dx has units. Probability is a pure number, but dx is a length in X's units, and that is what makes density a per-unit-length quantity. The re-test for next week: is the hours-to-minutes rescaling (height 2 vs height 1/30) still obvious? If yes, the density concept is durably in.

Why is E(X+Y) = E(X) + E(Y) with no independence assumption? My instinct said you need the distribution of X+Y first, and building that distribution means working out how X and Y interact. This note is the regrouping move that dissolved the itch, and the same move later turned out to prove LOTUS too. Setup Two fair coins. X = 1 if the first coin lands heads, else 0. Y the same for the second coin. The route I trusted: find the distribution of X+Y (values \{0,1,2\} with probabilities \{1/4, 1/2, 1/4\}, where the middle 1/2 comes from merging HT and TH), then E(X+Y) = 1. That merge step felt essential. It is where the two coins combine, so I assumed any proof of linearity had to pass through it. Now the second route. The sample space has four pebbles, HH, HT, TH, TT, each with weight 1/4. Sum directly over pebbles, never forming any distribution: E(X+Y) = \sum_s \big(X(s) + Y(s)\big)\,P(\{s\}) = 2 \cdot \tfrac14 + 1 \cdot \tfrac14 + 1 \cdot \tfrac14 + 0 \cdot \tfrac14 = 1. Each term splits as X(s)P(\{s\}) + Y(s)P(\{s\}), so the whole sum splits into two pebble sums, one for X and one for Y. Where I got stuck I refused to call those two sums E(X) and E(Y). The sum \sum_s X(s)P(\{s\}) runs over the four-pebble Cartesian-product world, but X was born on a two-outcome world with its own PMF. The underlying experiment changed, so why would a sum over the wrong sample space compute E(X)? I could feel the informal rescue (each P(\{s\}) shrank, and the number of pebbles grew in proportion, so it balances out) but I could not formalize it. The key move: group by value Take the X-part of the sum and, instead of adding left to right, collect the pebbles by the value X takes: \sum_s X(s)P(\{s\}) = 1 \cdot \big(\tfrac14 + \tfrac14\big) + 0 \cdot \big(\tfrac14 + \tfrac14\big) = 1 \cdot \tfrac12 + 0 \cdot \tfrac12. Inside each group X is constant, so it factors out. And each group's total weight is P(X = x) by definition, on whatever sample space X happens to live. That is the marginal probability, computed by pooling pebbles. So the pebble sum is \sum_x x\,P(X=x) = E(X), always. My "shrank but grew in proportion" intuition was this grouping, stated loosely. One correction to my first attempt at formalizing it: I leaned on "each x repeats |Y| times", which only works for this product-shaped example. The grouping argument needs no product structure and no equal weights. Any pebble world, same move. The picture to keep: expectation has two accounting systems. Pebble-by-pebble sums over outcomes, value-by-value sums over the PMF. They are the same sum with the terms regrouped, and regrouping a finite sum changes nothing. So you compute in whichever system is convenient, and equalities proven in one system transfer to the other for free. Payoff 1: linearity is unconditional The split (X(s)+Y(s))P(\{s\}) = X(s)P(\{s\}) + Y(s)P(\{s\}) happens per pebble, before any distribution is formed. No joint structure exists yet, so independence never gets consulted. The merge I thought was essential (HT and TH pooling into P(X+Y=1) = 1/2) is just the grouping move applied to the value of X+Y, and it happens after linearity is already settled. That is the whole reason E(X+Y) = E(X) + E(Y) holds for dependent variables too. Payoff 2: the same move is the LOTUS proof Group the pebbles by the value of g(X) instead of the value of X and you get LOTUS: E(g(X)) = \sum_x g(x)P(X=x). I did this by hand before knowing the theorem's name. Computing E(W) for W = (X-3.5)^2 on a die, I instinctively paired the six terms into three collision braces (x=1 with x=6, and so on), and each brace held a constant value of W with pooled weight \tfrac16 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac13 = P(W=w). The braces are super-pebbles. Same grouping, different sorting key. The full LOTUS story, including what it does not license, lives in lotus-and-variance. One move, two theorems: split before grouping gives linearity, group by g(X) gives LOTUS.

Chapter 3 swaps the language of events-as-sets for random variables, which are functions that turn outcomes into numbers. Once outcomes are numbers you can do arithmetic on them, and a distribution is the object that records how probability is spread across those numbers. Why Numbers Beat Sets Up to Chapter 2 an event is a set of outcomes, and the only tools are set operations: union, intersection, complement. That is limiting. You can intersect "it rains" with "I carry an umbrella", but you cannot add two events, or XOR them, or double one. There is no arithmetic on sets of outcomes. A random variable fixes this by mapping each outcome to a number: X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}. Now the outcomes are numbers, so X + Y, 2X, and X \oplus Y all mean something, and each is itself a new random variable. That is the real reason random variables exist: they let you build new quantities out of old ones. A random variable adds no randomness of its own. The randomness lives in the underlying experiment, the sample space \Omega. The variable relabels those outcomes as numbers, and in doing so it induces a new distribution on the numbers. Same randomness, new bookkeeping. The simplest kind is an indicator random variable, which is 1 when some event happens and 0 otherwise. It answers a yes/no question as a number, and adding up indicators is how you count events. The PMF: a Random Variable's Fingerprint A discrete random variable, one whose range is finite or countable, is fully described by its probability mass function: p_X(x) = P(X = x). Read P(X = x) as the probability of the event \{\omega : X(\omega) = x\}, all the outcomes the variable sends to x. The PMF lists, for each value the variable can take, how much probability lands there. Two conditions make a function a valid PMF. It is nonnegative, p_X(x) \ge 0 for every x, since probabilities cannot go below zero. And it sums to 1 over the support, \sum_x p_X(x) = 1, since the variable takes some value with certainty. The PMF is what people mean by "the distribution of a discrete random variable". Hand me the PMF and I know everything probabilistic about X. The Named Distributions Four distributions do most of the work in this chapter. Two are worth knowing cold. Bernoulli: one trial X \sim \text{Bern}(p) is a single trial with two outcomes, success and failure. It is the indicator of success: P(X = 1) = p, \qquad P(X = 0) = 1 - p. The failure probability 1 - p turns up so often it gets its own letter, q = 1 - p. That is the whole distribution. Every yes/no experiment with success chance p is a Bernoulli. Binomial: n independent trials X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p) counts the successes in n independent Bernoulli(p) trials, all sharing the same p: P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^{k} (1-p)^{n-k}. The story reads straight off the formula. The factor p^{k} q^{n-k} is the chance of one particular sequence with k successes, and \binom{n}{k} counts how many such sequences there are. When p = \tfrac{1}{2} the p^{k} q^{n-k} factor is the same 1/2^{n} for every k, so the shape is carried entirely by \binom{n}{k}. That makes \text{Bin}(n, \tfrac{1}{2}) symmetric, peaking in the middle and tapering to the edges. That peak is the same shape as a random walk's position and a two-dice sum, and why it peaks is worth its own note: random-walk-is-binomial. Discrete Uniform and Hypergeometric, in brief X \sim \text{DUnif}(C) spreads probability evenly over a finite set C, so P(X = x) = 1/|C| for each x \in C. It is the "no reason to prefer any value" baseline. X \sim \text{HGeom}(w, b, n) is the number of white items in a sample of n drawn without replacement from a jar of w white and b black. You pull n items in total, a mix of both colours, and X = k counts how many of them are white: P(X = k) = \frac{\binom{w}{k}\binom{b}{n-k}}{\binom{w+b}{n}}. The numerator reads straight off that story: pick which k of the w white items landed in the sample, \binom{w}{k}, and which n-k of the b black ones filled the rest, \binom{b}{n-k}, over all \binom{w+b}{n} ways to draw the sample. The one thing to hold onto is the contrast with Binomial. Binomial is sampling with replacement, so the draws are independent and p never moves. Hypergeometric is sampling without replacement, so each draw changes the composition of the jar and the draws are dependent. Reach for Binomial when the pool is effectively infinite, Hypergeometric when it is a fixed finite pool. Mixing them up is an easy slip: a "count the successes" problem is only Binomial if the trials are actually independent. A clean way to picture the Hypergeometric is that every item carries two tags, its type (white or black) and its status (sampled or not). The count k sits in the white-and-sampled cell. Swapping which tag you call "type" and which you call "sample" gives a distribution that reads differently but comes out equal. Why that symmetry holds is one I have parked in probability-open-questions. The CDF: One Descriptor for Everything The cumulative distribution function accumulates the PMF from the left: F_X(x) = P(X \le x). Its value at x is the total probability at or below x. The CDF is the universal descriptor because it is defined for every random variable, discrete or continuous, while the PMF only makes sense for discrete ones. It always climbs from 0 to 1 and never decreases. For a discrete variable the two hold the same information. The CDF is the running sum of the PMF, and the PMF is recovered as the size of each jump in the CDF, the jump at x being exactly p_X(x). Building New Random Variables Because a random variable is a function on \Omega, any function of it, g(X), is again a function on \Omega, so it is another random variable. X^{2}, 2X, and |X| are all random variables in their own right. This gives a handy technique for a variable whose distribution you do not recognize: express it as a one-to-one function of a variable you do know. A one-to-one g relabels the values without merging any of them, so each new value inherits the probability of the old one it came from. That is the trick behind the random walk, whose position is a one-to-one relabelling of a Binomial count, worked in random-walk-is-binomial. Two Category Errors to Avoid Blitzstein calls these "sympathetic magic": treating a random variable as if it were its distribution, or as if it were a plain number. Same PMF does not mean same variable Let X be the indicator of heads on one fair toss, and let Y = 1 - X. Both are \text{Bern}(\tfrac{1}{2}), so they have the identical PMF. They are still not the same random variable: on every outcome they disagree, since Y is 1 exactly when X is 0. The PMF is a summary of a variable, not the variable itself. The second slip is doubling. To get the PMF of 2X you cannot double the PMF of X. The values double, the probabilities do not. P(2X = 4) equals P(X = 2), since the probability stays with its outcome and only the label moves. Doubling the probabilities instead would not even leave them summing to 1. What's Still Shaky Three threads from this chapter I have not closed, parked in probability-open-questions: the Hypergeometric tag symmetry above, why the binomial coefficients across a row sum to 2^{n}, and whether X = Y as random variables forces them to map the underlying experiment identically. The deep dive on the peaked-distribution family lives in random-walk-is-binomial.

The Problem A particle starts at 0 on the number line and takes n steps. Each step is +1 or -1 with equal probability. After n steps, what is the distribution of its position? I worked it out by hand for the first few n. Some things jumped out of those P_{X_1}, P_{X_2}, P_{X_3} tables: After 1 step it sits on \pm 1. After 2 steps, only even positions. After 3 steps, only odd positions. The reachable set flips parity with n. Each distribution is symmetric about 0, with the most mass near 0 and less toward the edges. It looked like a bell, or like the triangle you get from summing two dice, which peaks at 7. What I could not do was jump to general n. Redoing the tree for every n is hopeless. I needed the position's PMF as a formula, and I did not see how to get there. Where I Got Stuck Those tables were positions: X_1 the position after one step, X_2 after two, X_3 after three. I was treating each one as a random variable whose distribution I did not know, and grinding it out by hand with a tree. The instinct was to keep going the same way for general n: build X_n's table too, so Y = X_n. That is the trap. Each new step splits every position into two, so the tree doubles and after n steps the bookkeeping explodes. Redoing it for every n is hopeless, and it hands me no formula for P(X_n = y). I was trying to compute the position's distribution in one piece, directly, instead of building it from simpler pieces I already understood. The Reframe: Count Rights, Not the Running Sum The way out is to build the position from simple pieces instead of computing it whole. Let X_i be the i-th step, +1 for a right and -1 for a left (reusing X_i, now for the step itself rather than the running position). Each step is a trivial fair two-outcome trial, and the position is just their sum: Y = X_1 + X_2 + \dots + X_n, \qquad X_i \in \{-1, +1\}. This is the reframe. Adding up n independent identical fair steps builds a Binomial, so Y is a Binomial in disguise and I never have to grind out its distribution by hand: I know one step, and Y is n of them summed. Whether I write a step as right or left, +1 or -1, or a 0/1 indicator, is just notation for the same coin. What is left is bookkeeping to pin down exactly which Binomial. That bookkeeping is cleanest if you stop tracking the running sum and count the two kinds of step instead. Let R be the number of right steps and L the number of left steps. Two facts then pin down everything: n = R + L, \qquad Y = R - L. The first says every step is either a right or a left. The second is the position, since each right adds 1 and each left subtracts 1. Now R is easy to name. Over n independent steps, each going right with probability 1/2, R is a count of successes in n fair trials. So R \sim \text{Bin}(n, 1/2) and P(R = r) = \binom{n}{r} \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{r} \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-r} = \binom{n}{r} \frac{1}{2^{n}}. Both probabilities are 1/2, so p^{r}(1-p)^{n-r} collapses to 1/2^{n} no matter what r is. The entire shape of the distribution is carried by the count \binom{n}{r} alone. From R to the Position y I still had the probability in terms of R, not the position y I actually care about. The same two equations bridge them. Adding n = R + L and Y = R - L drops L and gives R = \frac{n + y}{2}. Landing at position y forces exactly \frac{n+y}{2} of the steps to have been rights. Substitute: P(Y = y) = \binom{n}{\frac{n+y}{2}} \frac{1}{2^{n}}. That is the whole PMF. Two constraints fix its domain, and they explain the parity pattern I had noticed by hand: Parity. The count \frac{n+y}{2} has to be a whole number, so n + y must be even, so y shares the parity of n. Even n lands on even positions, odd n on odd positions, and off-parity positions get probability 0. Range. The number of rights runs 0 \le \frac{n+y}{2} \le n, which is just -n \le y \le n. You cannot get further from 0 than the number of steps you took. The textbook runs the same derivation in its random walk example (Example 3.7.2 in the 2nd edition), writing the position as Y = 2X - n with X \sim \text{Bin}(n, 1/2) counting the right steps. That is the same R - L in different letters, since X = R and n - X = L. Quick check against my hand tables: for n = 3, P(Y = 1) = \binom{3}{2}\frac{1}{8} = \frac{3}{8}, exactly the 3/8 I had written for position 1 under P_{X_3}. The Click: One Shape, Three Disguises Once the PMF is \binom{n}{(n+y)/2} / 2^{n}, the bell stops being a surprise. The 1/2^{n} is a constant. The whole shape is the binomial coefficient \binom{n}{k} swept across k, and I already knew that coefficient peaks in the middle and drops off toward the ends. Why the coefficient peaks Two arguments, and the second is the one worth keeping. Symmetry rules out a monotonic slide. Choosing k items to take is the same as choosing the n - k to leave behind, so \binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}. The values at k and n-k match, which forces a symmetric hump rather than a curve that just keeps falling. The ratio test says where the hump turns over. Compare one coefficient to the next: \frac{\binom{n}{k+1}}{\binom{n}{k}} = \frac{n-k}{k+1}. While this ratio is above 1, the sequence is still climbing. Setting \frac{n-k}{k+1} \ge 1 rearranges to n - k \ge k + 1, that is k \le \frac{n-1}{2}. So the coefficients grow up to about the middle and shrink after it. For even n there is a single peak at k = n/2. For odd n the ratio equals exactly 1 at the center, so the two middle values tie. The same shape everywhere Map that back to the walk. The count of rights is k = \frac{n+y}{2}, and \binom{n}{k} is largest at k = n/2. Setting \frac{n+y}{2} = \frac{n}{2} gives y = 0. The most likely place to end up is where you started, with the probability decaying symmetrically toward \pm n. That is the same peak, relabeled from "number of rights k" to "position y". It is also the same shape as summing two dice. There, middle sums like 7 have many more combinations (1{+}6, 2{+}5, 3{+}4, \dots) than edge sums like 2, which only comes from 1{+}1, so mass piles up in the center. Worth pinning down what that dice sum actually is. With X and Y the two dice, X + Y is not a Binomial. A die is uniform on \{1, \dots, 6\}, not a Bernoulli, so the sum is a triangular distribution, the convolution of two uniforms, which is why its plot has straight sides rather than a smooth hump. It shares the Binomial's shape through the mechanism, not the formula: both are sums of independent identical pieces, and summing independent pieces piles mass in the middle, since more input pairs land on the central values. The walk lands on the Binomial exactly because its pieces are \pm 1 Bernoulli steps, while the dice sum lands on a triangle because its pieces are uniform. Same family, different members. Binomial coefficients, dice sums, and the random walk are the same peaked, symmetric object wearing different labels. The random-walk PMF is a relabeled \text{Bin}(n, 1/2), and nothing more. The reason it keeps smoothing toward a cleaner bell as n grows has a name, the Central Limit Theorem: a sum of many independent identical pieces tends toward a bell whatever the pieces look like, and the walk is exactly such a sum. Aside: y on Both Sides Is Fine For a while the formula bothered me because y shows up on the left and the right of P(Y = y) = \dots. That looked like an equation I should solve for y. It is not. P(Y = y) is a function definition, read as "the probability that the random variable Y takes the specific value y". Capital Y is the random variable, lowercase y is a particular number you plug in, and the PMF is often written p_Y(y) to make that explicit. It is no stranger than f(x) = x^2 having x on both sides. That capital-vs-lowercase split is exactly the machinery behind probability-distributions-and-random-variables.

What's Vague About "Big O" I knew the labels: O(n) is linear, O(\log n) is logarithmic, O(2^n) is exponential. I could rank them. But I couldn't explain what asymptotic analysis is actually doing, or why the formal definitions are written the way they are. Why do we throw away constants? What's the n_0 in the definition? Why is there both a "Big O" and a "little o"? The missing piece was connecting asymptotic notation to derivatives. The Slope Perspective Asymptotic analysis compares how fast the slopes of two functions grow. Given f(n) and g(n), compute their derivatives f'(n) and g'(n). Whichever derivative grows faster will eventually dominate, regardless of what happens at small inputs. Three cases: Constant slope (f(n) = n, so f'(n) = 1): effort grows steadily. Each additional input costs the same. Accelerating slope (f(n) = n^2, so f'(n) = 2n): effort accelerates. Each additional input costs more than the last. Decelerating slope (f(n) = \log n, so f'(n) = 1/n): effort flattens out. Even for a trillion inputs, \log_2(10^{12}) \approx 40. This is the whole game. When we say n^2 "grows faster" than 100n, we mean the slope of n^2 (which is 2n) eventually outpaces the slope of 100n (which is just 100). No constant multiplier can prevent this, because a growing function always beats a constant. Why Constants Get Thrown Away Take f(n) = 100n and g(n) = n^2. At n = 5: f(5) = 500 and g(5) = 25. The linear function looks way worse. At n = 1000: f(1000) = 10^5 and g(1000) = 10^6. The quadratic function is 10x worse. The crossover happens at n = 100 (where 100n = n^2). Before that, the constant inflates f above g. After that, the accelerating slope of n^2 takes over permanently. The constant 100 only delays the crossover point. It can't prevent it, because g'(n) = 2n keeps growing while f'(n) = 100 stays flat. Even 10^9 \cdot n would eventually lose to n^2, it would just take until n = 10^9 for the crossover to happen. That's why we write O(n) instead of O(100n). The constant changes when the crossover occurs, not whether it occurs. The Formal Definitions All four notations classify the relative growth relationship between two functions. The slope perspective connects them all. Big O (O): the loose ceiling (\le). f(n) is O(g(n)) if there exist constants c and n_0 such that for all n \ge n_0: f(n) \le c \cdot g(n). The n_0 is the crossover point. We're saying "I don't care about the messy race at small inputs, I only care about behavior after the curves diverge." The c absorbs the constant factor we're throwing away. This allows ties: 2n is O(n) because they have the same growth shape. Little o (o): the strict gap (<). f(n) is o(g(n)) if \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{f(n)}{g(n)} = 0. Big O allows two functions with the same growth shape (like 2n and n). Little o demands that f becomes insignificant compared to g. The ratio has to go to zero, not just stay bounded. So n is o(n^2) (linear is negligible compared to quadratic), but 2n is NOT o(n) (their ratio is 2, not 0). Little o means g's slope is in a completely higher league. Big Omega (\Omega): the floor (\ge). f(n) is \Omega(g(n)) if f(n) \ge c \cdot g(n) for all n > n_0. The mirror of Big O. Instead of "won't grow faster than this," it says "won't grow slower than this." In security, we use this to prove a lower bound on the attacker's work: their effort is at least exponential. Theta (\Theta): the exact fit (=). f(n) is \Theta(g(n)) if it is both O(g(n)) and \Omega(g(n)). The growth shape is pinned down exactly. It's both the ceiling and the floor. NotationIntuitionAnalogyO(g(n))Loose ceiling\le (allows ties)o(g(n))Strict gap< (no ties)\Omega(g(n))Floor\ge\Theta(g(n))Exact fit= Worst case vs average case. Big O usually describes worst-case complexity (Murphy's Law: assume the input is the absolute worst arrangement). Average case measures expected time over a randomly chosen input. In security, worst-case matters because we assume the attacker is brilliant and lucky. The Caveat: Asymptotics vs Practice An algorithm that is asymptotically better isn't always better in practice. If we're only processing 50 items, an O(n \log n) algorithm with a constant factor of 1000 is slower than an O(n^2) algorithm with a constant factor of 1. The constants we threw away dominate at small inputs. Asymptotic analysis assumes n is massive. For small or moderate n, you have to look at the actual constants and benchmark. Where This Shows Up in Security Cryptographic security is built on an asymmetric gap between two growth curves. We want the legitimate user's effort to be polynomial (O(n) or O(\log n)), while forcing the attacker into exponential effort (O(2^n)). Adding 1 bit to a key doubles the attacker's work (2^{n+1} = 2 \cdot 2^n), but barely changes the user's effort. That's the asymmetry. In the formal notation: the user's effort is o of the attacker's effort (strict gap, not just Big O). The ratio \frac{\log n}{2^n} \to 0, so the user becomes negligible compared to the attacker's workload as n grows. The threat is shortcuts. If someone discovers an O(n^3) algorithm for factoring (replacing the current exponential methods), the gap collapses. Both user and attacker would be in polynomial time, and the "wall" disappears. This is exactly the quantum computing concern with RSA. For how this asymptotic gap gets formalized into security definitions, see why-negligible-funcs (negligible functions are the functions that shrink faster than any inverse polynomial, making polynomial repetition unable to amplify success) and hardness-assumption (the assumption that no polynomial-time algorithm can solve the underlying problem).

The Euclidean algorithm replaces the pair (a, b) by (b, r), where a = q b + r and 0 \le r < b, and repeats until the remainder is 0. It computes \gcd(a, b) only if every step preserves it: \gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, r). Where I got stuck Picture a as a strip cut into q segments of length b and a leftover of length r. Let d = \gcd(a, b), the biggest block that tiles both a and b. The block d tiles the whole strip and tiles each b segment, so it tiles the leftover: r = a - q b = (k_1 - q k_2)\, d . So d divides both b and r. I read that as "d is the gcd of (b, r) as well", equality, done. When the write-up said this only proves \gcd(a, b) \le \gcd(b, r), I pushed back for three turns. I had started with d being the gcd, not some factor, so where could an inequality come from? What the argument actually used One property of d: it divides a and b. It never used that d is the largest such number. So any block with that property survives the same argument, and the conclusion is only what is true of every such block: d is a common divisor of (b, r). Being the gcd of (a, b) is a fact about the pair (a, b). It says nothing about how the pair (b, r) ranks its divisors. The counterexample is to the inference, not to the number. Take a = 24, b = 18, so 24 = 1 \cdot 18 + 6. The block 3 tiles 24 and 18, so by the same argument it tiles r = 6. All true, and \gcd(18, 6) = 6, not 3. The argument's shape cannot tell 3 from 6, so it cannot conclude "greatest" for either. What the strip argument proves, exactly: every common divisor of (a, b) is a common divisor of (b, r). Hence \gcd(a, b) \le \gcd(b, r), and nothing more. The other direction The way it closed: suppose (b, r) had a common divisor e bigger than d. Then e divides b and r, so it divides q b + r = a. That makes e a common divisor of (a, b) bigger than the greatest one, which is impossible. So no common divisor of (b, r) exceeds d, and with the first half that is equality. Written out directly it is the same line. Take any e dividing both b and r, say b = e m_1 and r = e m_2. Then a = q b + r = e\,(q m_1 + m_2), so e divides a too. Every common divisor of (b, r) is a common divisor of (a, b), which gives \gcd(b, r) \le \gcd(a, b). The two directions use different halves of the same equation. The first subtracts, r = a - q b, and the second adds back, a = q b + r. Each is one line, and neither alone is the lemma. On the counterexample pair the chain runs (24, 18) \to (18, 6) \to (6, 0) with gcd 6 at every stage. On a coprime pair, (12, 5) \to (5, 2) \to (2, 1) \to (1, 0), the gcd is 1 throughout, which is what makes the back-substitution in units-mod-n-coprime-and-totient land on 1. The general lesson: an argument that uses only a shared property cannot single out the extreme element. To prove "d is the greatest" the word greatest has to enter somewhere, and here it enters only through the reverse direction. Same shape as one-to-one-proof-converse-trap: one direction proved, both directions claimed. Mantra "Tiles both" makes it a factor. "Greatest" needs the other direction.

Statement Let p be any prime and a any integer not divisible by p. Then a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p} There's a more general form, a^p \equiv a \pmod{p}, which includes the trivial case when p \mid a. Both are equivalent, the second just doesn't require the coprimality condition. Proof Setup Consider (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^* = \{1, 2, \ldots, p-1\} and pick some a \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}^*. Define a map f: \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}^* 	o \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}^* by f(x) = a \cdot x So f sends the group elements \{1, 2, \ldots, p-1\} to \{a \cdot 1, a \cdot 2, \ldots, a \cdot (p-1)\}. f is a bijection Surjective: Since p is prime, a^{-1} exists and is unique in \mod p. For any element a \cdot i in the image, there's a pre-image a^{-1} \cdot a \cdot i = i. Injective: Suppose f(i) = f(j), meaning a \cdot i \equiv a \cdot j \pmod{p}. Multiply both sides by a^{-1}: So i 
eq j \implies f(i) 
eq f(j). f is NOT an automorphism. It doesn't preserve the group operation, i.e., f(i \cdot j) 
eq f(i) \cdot f(j). All f does is permute the group elements. The punchline Since f is a bijection on a finite set, it's just a permutation. The product of all group elements stays the same: The last step cancels \prod i from both sides. Every element in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^* is coprime to p, so it's invertible. Extension to Euler's theorem This generalizes to Euler's theorem: a^{\varphi(m)} \equiv 1 \pmod{m} where \gcd(a, m) = 1. Replace (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^* with \mathbb{Z}_m^* = \{x \in \mathbb{Z}_m : \gcd(x, m) = 1\}. The map f(x) = a \cdot x is still a bijection on this group, so the product argument carries over, just with \varphi(m) elements instead of p - 1.

Security Game The adversary \mathcal{A} picks two messages m_0, m_1 \in \{0, 1\} and sends them to the challenger. The challenger samples k \xleftarrow{\text{\textdollar}} \{0, 1\} and b \xleftarrow{\text{\textdollar}} \{0, 1\}, computes c_b = k \oplus m_b, and sends the ciphertext back to the adversary. The adversary then outputs a guess b'. We want to show that \text{Adv}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\text{distinguishcipher}} = 0 for the one-time pad. Setting Up the Probability The advantage is defined in terms of \Pr[b' = b]. Expanding by cases on b: Where I Got Stuck I couldn't figure out how to reason about the two conditional probabilities \Pr[b'=1 \mid b=1] and \Pr[b'=0 \mid b=0], because the adversary is the one choosing b'. Depending on the adversary, it could always output b'=1, or always output b'=0, or flip a fair coin internally, or run some fancy function of the ciphertext. Since the proof needs to work for all adversaries, I didn't know how to assign a concrete value to those probabilities. They seemed completely under the adversary's control, not something I could calculate from the game description alone. The Key Move: Condition on the Key The trick is to not think about what the adversary "decides" to do, but instead condition on the random variable the adversary actually sees, which is the ciphertext. And the ciphertext depends on the key k. Expanding \Pr[b'=1 \mid b=1] by conditioning on k: Similarly for the other term: The adversary's behavior reduces to a deterministic function of its input. We don't need to know what the adversary does. We just need to know that for any fixed input x, \Pr[\mathcal{A}(x) = 1] + \Pr[\mathcal{A}(x) = 0] = 1. The Two Cases Claim: \Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 1] + \Pr[b' = 0 \mid b = 0] = 1, regardless of the adversary's strategy. Case 1: The adversary chooses m_0 = m_1. Then 1 \oplus m_0 = 1 \oplus m_1, so the matching pairs are: \Pr[\mathcal{A}(m_1) = 1] + \Pr[\mathcal{A}(m_0) = 0] = 1 \Pr[\mathcal{A}(1 \oplus m_1) = 1] + \Pr[\mathcal{A}(1 \oplus m_0) = 0] = 1 Case 2: The adversary chooses m_0 \ne m_1. Since the message space is \{0,1\}, one message is 0 and the other is 1, so m_1 = 1 \oplus m_0. The matching pairs cross over: \Pr[\mathcal{A}(m_1) = 1] + \Pr[\mathcal{A}(1 \oplus m_0) = 0] = 1 \Pr[\mathcal{A}(1 \oplus m_1) = 1] + \Pr[\mathcal{A}(m_0) = 0] = 1 In both cases, the weighted sum gives exactly 1. So: The advantage is 2 \cdot \Pr[b'=b] - 1 = 0. The one-time pad gives the adversary no information, no matter what strategy it uses.

A residue a has a multiplicative inverse mod n exactly when the greatest common divisor (gcd) of a and n is 1. The invertible residues form a group, the unit group (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times, and it has \varphi(n) elements. Start with n = 6 Which of 1 to 5 have an inverse mod 6? Multiply and look for a 1. Since 1 \cdot 1 = 1 and 5 \cdot 5 = 25 \equiv 1, both 1 and 5 are units. The residue 1 is a unit for every n and is its own inverse, since \gcd(1, n) = 1. The other three never reach 1: 2 \cdot 3 = 6 \equiv 0, 3 \cdot 2 \equiv 0, 4 \cdot 3 = 12 \equiv 0. Once a product hits 0 the row of products just cycles. The rule is not "n divides a": 6 does not divide 4, and 4 still fails. The rule is that a and n share a factor. 4 shares the factor 2 with 6, and a shared factor is enough to kill the inverse. An inverse is a combination equal to 1 Write out what an inverse means. a k \equiv 1 \pmod n says a k = 1 + q n for some integer q, so a k - q n = 1 . So "does a have an inverse" is the same question as "can I build 1 out of a and n with integer coefficients". Bézout's identity is the name for the fact that the smallest positive number you can build this way is \gcd(a, n). The two directions below are that identity, proved on the pair we care about. Shared factor means no inverse Let d = \gcd(a, n) and write a = k_1 d, n = k_2 d. Then every combination is a k - n q = (k k_1 - q k_2)\, d . Every combination is a whole number of copies of d. If d > 1 the combination can never equal 1, so there is no inverse. That is the "only if" direction. Coprime means an inverse exists: run Euclid backwards Take a = 5 and n = 12. Divide with remainder, then divide the divisor by the remainder, until the remainder is 0: The last nonzero remainder is 1, and the goal is to write that 1 as a combination of 12 and 5. The first equation already does this for its own remainder: 2 = 12 - 2 \cdot 5. The second equation contains that 2, so substitute, and its remainder 1 becomes a combination of 12 and 5 as well: Reduce mod 12 and the 12 \cdot 2 term vanishes: 5 \cdot 5 \equiv 1, so 5 is its own inverse mod 12. The general idea is a chain of substitutions. The first equation holds a, n and a remainder. The remainder has coefficient 1 in its own equation, so solving for it writes the remainder as a combination of a and n. Substitute that into the next equation, and its remainder is a combination of a and n too. Repeat down the chain. The last equation then reads \gcd(a, n) = a x + n y, and for coprime a and n that is 1 = a x + n y, with x the inverse. This is the extended Euclidean algorithm. Tracking x and y step by step, rather than by substitution, is the follow-up in extended-euclidean-algorithm-study. Two claims carry this proof and both need checking: each Euclid step keeps the gcd, and the chain stops exactly at the gcd. Each Euclid step keeps the gcd One step is a = q b + r with 0 \le r < b. The claim is \gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, r). First half. Let d = \gcd(a, b), so a = k_1 d and b = k_2 d. Picture a strip of length a cut into q segments of length b and a leftover of length r. The block d tiles the whole strip and tiles each b segment, so it must tile the leftover: r = a - q b = (k_1 - q k_2)\, d . So d is a common divisor of b and r, and that is all it is so far. The block d is the greatest common divisor of (a, b). Nothing above says it is the greatest common divisor of (b, r), only that it is a factor of both. Being the gcd of the first pair does not make it the gcd of the second. What this half proves is \gcd(a, b) \le \gcd(b, r). Second half. Take any e dividing both b and r, say b = e m_1 and r = e m_2. Then a = q b + r = e\,(q m_1 + m_2), so e divides a as well. Every common divisor of (b, r) is a common divisor of (a, b), which gives \gcd(b, r) \le \gcd(a, b). The two inequalities together give equality. The trap in the one-sided version is its own note: euclid-step-keeps-gcd. Why the chain stops at the gcd The remainders are non-negative and strictly decreasing, since r < b at every step, so the chain reaches 0 after finitely many steps. The last line reads r_{k-1} = q \cdot r_k + 0, and \gcd(r_k, 0) = r_k, because every integer divides 0. Chain the lemma back up the lines and \gcd(a, n) = \gcd(r_k, 0) = r_k. The last nonzero remainder is the gcd. When a and n are coprime that remainder is 1, which is exactly what the back-substitution builds. Repetition Amplifies Polynomial Success Rates Say an attacker breaks a scheme with probability \epsilon in a single attempt, where \epsilon is some non-negligible function of the security parameter n (for example, \epsilon = 1/n^2). If the attacker repeats the experiment q times independently, the probability of failing every single time is: (1 - \epsilon)^q Since (1 - \epsilon) is strictly less than 1, multiplying it by itself q times makes it continuously decrease. So the success probability 1 - (1 - \epsilon)^q keeps growing toward 1. With a polynomial base success rate, this actually works. If \epsilon = 1/n^2 and the attacker runs q = n^2 experiments, the total success probability is roughly n^2 \cdot 1/n^2 = 1. That's a guaranteed break. Where This Gets Confusing So what about making \epsilon really small? If the attacker has a 0.0001\% chance of success, the same logic still applies. Repeating the experiment enough times drives the failure probability toward zero. The math doesn't care how small \epsilon is, only that (1 - \epsilon) < 1. I couldn't see why defining a special class of "negligible" functions would change anything. Multiplying a number less than 1 by itself always decreases it. What makes negligible different? The Asymptotic Race The answer isn't that the failure probability stops decreasing. It does decrease. The point is that the attacker is computationally bounded and can only run polynomially many experiments. Modern cryptography limits the base success probability to a negligible function \text{negl}(n), defined as a function that shrinks faster than the inverse of any positive polynomial. For any polynomial p(n), there exists N such that for all n > N: \text{negl}(n) < \frac{1}{p(n)} In practice, negligible functions shrink exponentially (like 2^{-n}). A polynomial-time attacker is limited to q(n) repetitions where q(n) is some polynomial. Their total success probability is bounded by: q(n) \cdot \text{negl}(n) For example, n^{10} \cdot 2^{-n}. As n grows, 2^{-n} crushes n^{10}. The product goes to zero no matter how large the polynomial exponent is. This is why the definition works: a polynomial \epsilon (like 1/n^2) can be amplified to near-certainty with polynomially many tries. A negligible \epsilon cannot. Polynomial repetitions can't outpace exponential shrinkage. Why Cryptographers Prove Bounds, Not Exact Probabilities Security proofs don't compute the exact success probability of an attacker. They prove that a worst-case ceiling is negligible, and that's enough. The Union Bound. If an attacker has q tries, each with success probability \text{negl}(n), the probability of succeeding at least once is bounded by: P(\text{at least one success}) \le q \cdot \text{negl}(n) Since polynomial \times negligible is still negligible, the ceiling stays negligible. That's the whole argument. Why the bound is tight (the binomial approximation). The exact probability of at least one success in q independent tries is 1 - (1 - \epsilon)^q where \epsilon = \text{negl}(n). Expanding (1 - \epsilon)^q via the binomial theorem: 1 - q\epsilon + \frac{q(q-1)}{2}\epsilon^2 - \frac{q(q-1)(q-2)}{6}\epsilon^3 + \cdots Substituting back into 1 - (1 - \epsilon)^q: q\epsilon - \frac{q(q-1)}{2}\epsilon^2 + \cdots Because \epsilon is astronomically small (say 2^{-256}), higher-order terms like \epsilon^2 and \epsilon^3 vanish. The dominant surviving term is q\epsilon. So the Union Bound q \cdot \text{negl}(n) isn't just a valid ceiling, it's a very tight approximation of the exact value. Why we still prefer the bound over the exact formula. The binomial formula 1 - (1 - \epsilon)^q assumes every attempt is perfectly independent. Real attackers use adaptive strategies: if the first query fails, they analyze that failure to craft a better second query. When trials are dependent, the binomial math breaks down entirely. The Union Bound holds even for dependent events. No matter how the attacker correlates their queries or learns from past failures, the total success probability is trapped below q \cdot \text{negl}(n).
